lead: In empty space, with no charges and no currents, Maxwell's four equations still allow a self-sustaining disturbance: a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, which makes an electric field again, and the pattern travels forward at c = 3×10⁸ m/s. The two fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, and they carry energy, momentum and pressure in a direction given by E × B. Every wireless link works on this: FM radio, Wi-Fi, a phone call on a Chennai street, radar, satellite TV, and the sunlight reaching a solar panel.
prereq: You need: Maxwell's equations and boundary conditions from Chapter 3.8, Faraday's law from Chapter 3.7, and the wave equation from Unit 2.

sections.h3: From Maxwell's equations to a wave equation

blocks.text: In empty space there is no charge and no current, so ρ = 0 and J = 0. Two equations then carry the whole story. Faraday's law says a changing magnetic field curls an electric field: ∇×E = −∂B/∂t. Ampere–Maxwell says a changing electric field curls a magnetic field: ∇×B = μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t. Each field generates the other, so a disturbance can keep itself alive with no charge to carry it.

items: Take the curl of Faraday's law: ∇×(∇×E) = −∂(∇×B)/∂t.
Put Ampere–Maxwell into the right side: ∇×(∇×E) = −μ₀ε₀ ∂²E/∂t².
Use the identity ∇×(∇×E) = ∇(∇·E) − ∇²E. In free space ∇·E = 0, so the first term dies.
Left with ∇²E = μ₀ε₀ ∂²E/∂t². The same steps on B give ∇²B = μ₀ε₀ ∂²B/∂t².

blocks.where: E is the electric field (V/m), ∇² is the Laplacian (second derivatives in x, y, z), t is time (s), μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m is the permeability of free space, ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m is the permittivity of free space, and c is the wave speed (m/s).

blocks.text: This has the same shape as the wave equation ∇²ψ = (1/v²) ∂²ψ/∂t² from Unit 2, with v = 1/√(μ₀ε₀). The numbers give c = 2.998×10⁸ m/s, the measured speed of light. Light is an electromagnetic wave.
Inside a medium, μ₀ becomes μ = μ₀μ_r and ε₀ becomes ε = ε₀ε_r, so v = 1/√(με) = c/n, where n = √(μ_rε_r) is the refractive index. For ordinary non-magnetic glass μ_r ≈ 1, so n ≈ √ε_r.

sections.h3: The plane wave: transverse, in phase, right-handed

blocks.text: The simplest solution is a plane wave: E has one value over any plane perpendicular to the direction of travel, and changes only along that direction and with time. Let the wave travel along +z.
E = E₀ sin(kz − ωt) along x,   B = B₀ sin(kz − ωt) along y
blocks.where: E₀ is the peak electric field (V/m), B₀ the peak magnetic field (T), k = 2π/λ is the wave number (rad/m) with λ the wavelength (m), ω = 2πf is the angular frequency (rad/s) with f the frequency (Hz), z is position (m) and t is time (s).

blocks.text: Three facts follow, and each one is worth a mark.

items: Transverse: ∇·E = 0 and ∇·B = 0 force both fields to lie in the wavefront plane, so neither has a component along z.
In phase, with fixed ratio: Faraday's law gives E₀/B₀ = c (or v in a medium). Both peak at the same instant.
Right-handed set: E × B points along the direction of travel. With E along x and B along y, E × B is along +z.

blocks.text: The phase kz − ωt stays constant when dz/dt = ω/k, so the pattern moves at the speed found above and ω = ck. In terms of frequency and wavelength, λ = c/f.

A wave carries energy. The electric field stores ½ε₀E² per unit volume (J/m³) and the magnetic field stores B²/(2μ₀). Since B = E/c the two are equal, so the total energy density is u = ε₀E², averaging to u_avg = ½ε₀E₀² over a cycle.

blocks.where: S is the Poynting vector (W/m²), the energy crossing unit area per second in the direction of E × B; H = B/μ₀ is the magnetic field strength (A/m); μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m.

blocks.text: S swings between 0 and a peak twice per cycle. Meters and antennas respond to its average, the intensity:

blocks.where: I is the intensity (W/m²), E₀ the peak electric field (V/m), B₀ the peak magnetic field (T), c = 3×10⁸ m/s and u_avg the average energy density (J/m³).

blocks.text: Energy moving at speed c also carries momentum: the momentum density is S/c². A surface that absorbs the wave feels a pressure I/c; a perfect reflector feels 2I/c. Sunlight at 1.4 kW/m² pushes with about 4.7 μPa, small on a hand but useful on a solar sail over months.

sections.h3: Production by a dipole antenna and reception by a phone

blocks.text: A charge at rest makes a static field. A charge shaken up and down at frequency f makes fields that change at f; far from the antenna they detach and travel as a transverse wave of that same frequency. That is the oscillating dipole antenna: a straight rod with electrons sloshing between its ends. Wavelength follows from λ = c/f, and the rod radiates best when its length is about λ/2 — a half-wave dipole.

An FM station at 100 MHz radiates λ = 3 m, so its tower is a few metres tall. A phone at 1800 MHz works with λ ≈ 17 cm, so a half-wave antenna around 8 cm fits inside the handset. Reception is the reverse: the electric field of the passing wave drives electrons along the phone's antenna, making a tiny voltage at the same frequency, which the receiver amplifies, filters and decodes.
At a boundary between two media, the four boundary conditions of Chapter 3.8 decide how much of the wave reflects and how much bends; Unit 4 works out reflection and refraction of light from them.

figure.caption: E and B rise and fall together as the wave moves along z; the magnetic curve is drawn at half height only so both curves can be seen. The curves never separate, which is the in-phase condition of a plane wave.

spec.aria: Two sine curves along the z axis, electric field at full height and magnetic field at half height, rising and falling together.

examples.question: A plane electromagnetic wave in free space travels along +z with its electric field along x and peak value E₀ = 30 V/m. Take ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m, μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m and c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s. Find (a) the peak magnetic field B₀ and its direction, (b) the average intensity I, (c) the average energy density u_avg, and check that u_avg × c returns I.
steps: In a plane wave in free space E₀/B₀ = c, so B₀ = E₀/c.
B₀ = 30/(3.0×10⁸) = 1.0×10⁻⁷ T. It points along y, because E × B must point along +z.
For the intensity, first square the field: E₀² = 30² = 900 (V/m)².
Average energy density: u_avg = ½ε₀E₀² = 4.427×10⁻¹² × 900 = 3.98×10⁻⁹ J/m³.
Check: u_avg × c = 3.98×10⁻⁹ × 3.0×10⁸ = 1.195 W/m², the same intensity.
examples.answer: B₀ = 1.0×10⁻⁷ T along y, I ≈ 1.2 W/m², u_avg = 3.98×10⁻⁹ J/m³, and u_avg × c equals the same 1.2 W/m².
examples.check:
E0 = 30.0
c = 3.0e8
eps0 = 8.854e-12
B0 = E0 / c
I = 0.5 * eps0 * c * E0**2
u = 0.5 * eps0 * E0**2
print(round(B0, 10))
print(round(I, 2))
print(round(u, 11))

traps: Writing B₀ = cE₀. The magnetic field is weaker by the factor c: B₀ = E₀/c = E₀/3×10⁸.
Using ε₀cE₀² for the average intensity. The average of sin² is ½, so it is ½ε₀cE₀²; equivalently I = ε₀cE_rms² with E_rms = E₀/√2.
Saying E and B are 90° out of phase. In a plane wave in free space they peak together; a phase difference appears only in a conducting medium or in a standing wave.
Putting the free-space constants into a medium. Use ε = ε₀ε_r and μ, and then v = c/n, not c.
Calling E × B itself the Poynting vector. It is S = E × H = E × B/μ₀, measured in W/m².

quiz.q: State the two Maxwell equations that combine in free space to give the electromagnetic wave equation, and give the speed they predict.
quiz.a: Faraday's law ∇×E = −∂B/∂t and Ampere–Maxwell ∇×B = μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t. Combining them gives ∇²E = μ₀ε₀ ∂²E/∂t², so v = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = 3×10⁸ m/s.

quiz.q: Why must an electromagnetic wave in empty space be transverse?
quiz.a: In empty space ρ = 0, so Gauss's laws give ∇·E = 0 and ∇·B = 0. For a plane wave travelling along z the fields vary only with z, so ∂E_z/∂z = 0 and ∂B_z/∂z = 0: a constant longitudinal part is not a wave, leaving no field component along the direction of travel.

quiz.q: A plane wave in free space has peak electric field 100 V/m. Find the peak magnetic field and the average intensity. (ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m, c = 3×10⁸ m/s.)
Sunlight of intensity 1.4 kW/m² falls normally on a blackened plate that absorbs all of it. Find the radiation pressure on the plate.
quiz.a: For full absorption p = I/c = 1400/(3×10⁸) = 4.7×10⁻⁶ Pa. If the plate were a perfect reflector the pressure would be twice this, 9.3×10⁻⁶ Pa.

quiz.q: A wave of frequency f enters glass of refractive index 1.5 from air. Which of speed, frequency and wavelength change, and by what factor?
quiz.a: Frequency is set by the source and does not change. Speed falls to v = c/1.5 = 2×10⁸ m/s and wavelength falls by the same factor, λ = λ_air/1.5. The relation ω = vk still holds, with the new v.

quiz.q: In a plane wave the electric field is along +y and the wave travels along +z. Find the direction of B and of the energy flow, and justify it with E × B.
quiz.a: E × B must point along +z. Since ŷ × (−x̂) = +ẑ, B points along −x. The Poynting vector S = E × H points along +z, the direction of travel, so energy flows the way the wave moves.

beyond: Not for the exam. Radiation pressure is now a working technology: solar sails, optical tweezers that hold a single living cell, and laser cooling of atoms all use the momentum that light carries. In research the Poynting vector is split into spin and orbital parts to describe light carrying angular momentum, and near-field probes map energy flow around nanostructures smaller than a wavelength. Engineers designing 5G millimetre-wave links and satellite dishes solve this same wave equation with conducting boundaries added. Useful search words: optical tweezers, spin angular momentum of light, half-wave dipole radiation pattern.
